An amusing aside from a recent paper of mine (https://aten.cool/documents/papers/A%20rock-paper-scissors%20Mandelbrot%20set%20[2026].pdf):

Given a set \(A\) and a binary operation \(f\colon A^2\to A\), we refer to \((A,f)\) as a magma. Each magma has a magma algebra. The magma algebra for \((A,f)\) consists of all \(\mathbb{R}\)-linear combinations of (finitely many) elements of \(A\). This structure also inherits a bilinear multiplication from \((A,f)\), where we set
    \[
        \left(\sum_{x\in A}u_xx\right)\left(\sum_{y\in A}v_yy\right)=\sum_{(x,y)\in A^2}u_xv_yf(x,y).
    \]

The Cayley-Dickson algebras (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Dickson_construction) are a familiar family of real algebras which include the real numbers, the complex numbers, the quaternions, and the octonions, among others. Are any of the Cayley-Dickson algebras magma algebras? Certainly there is one example: The real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) are the magma algebra for the trivial magma where \(A\) has only a single element.
